18   II.  LEGAL STANDARD                                                   
19        As this action is premised on federal question jurisdiction, federal common law governs 
20   issues of privilege.  Fed. R. Evid. 501; United States v. Ruehle, 583 F.3d 600, 608 (9th Cir. 2009). 
21        “The attorney-client privilege protects confidential communications between attorneys and 
22   clients, which are made for the purpose of giving legal advice.”  United States v. Sanmina Corp., 
23   968 F.3d 1107, 1116 (9th Cir. 2020).  The privilege extends to a client’s confidential disclosures 
24   to an attorney in order to obtain legal advice, as well as an attorney’s advice in response to such 
25   disclosures.  Ruehle, 583 F.3d at 607 (citations and quotations omitted). The party claiming the 
26                                                                         
    2 For purposes of this motion, Valeo does not challenge individual entries on NVIDIA’s privilege 
27                                                                         
    log or NVIDIA’s compliance with the requirements of Rule 26(b)(5) and the Ninth Circuit’s 
1   privilege has the burden to establish that it applies.  See United States v. Martin, 278 F.3d 988, 
2   999–1000 (9th Cir. 2002).                                             
3        The attorney work product doctrine protects from discovery documents and tangible things 
4   prepared by a party or his representative in anticipation of litigation or for trial.  Fed. R. Civ. P. 
5   26(b)(3); Sanmina, 968 F.3d at 1119 (citation omitted).  “At its core, the work-product doctrine 
6   shelters the mental processes of the attorney, providing a privileged area within which he can 
7   analyze and prepare his client’s case.”  United States v. Nobles, 422 U.S. 225, 238 (1975).  The 
8   doctrine protects both “material prepared by agents for the attorney as well as those prepared by 
9   the attorney himself,” id. at 238-39, and its primary purpose is to “prevent exploitation of a party’s 
10   efforts in preparing for litigation,” Admiral Ins. Co. v. U.S. Dist. Ct., 881 F.2d 1486, 1494 (9th Cir. 
11   1989).  Typically, work product protection extends to interview notes, memoranda, summaries, 
12   and analyses, as well as to verbatim witness statements.  See Hickman v. Taylor, 329 U.S. 495, 
13   511 (1947); Hatamian v. Advanced Micro Devices, Inc., No. 14-cv-00226-YGR (JSC), 2016 WL 
14   2606830, at *3 (N.D. Cal. May 6, 2016).  A party asserting work product protection bears the 
15   burden of demonstrating that the protection applies.  See, e.g., Visa U.S.A., Inc. v. First Data 
16   Corp., No. C-02-1786 JSW (EMC), 2004 WL 1878209, at *5 (N.D. Cal. Aug. 23, 2004). 
17        The protections afforded by the attorney-client privilege and the work product doctrine are 
18   not absolute.  The attorney-client privilege may be waived expressly or by implication.  A party 
19   “may implicitly waive the privilege by asserting a claim or defense that relies on privileged 
20   materials as its basis.”  Dukes v. Wal-Mart Stores, Inc., No. 01-cv-2252 CRB (JSC), 2013 WL 
21   1282892, at *6 (N.D. Cal. Mar. 26, 2013) (citing Weil v. Inv./Indicators, Research & Mgmt., 647 
22   F.2d 18, 24 (9th Cir. 1981)). “In practical terms, this means that parties in litigation may not abuse 
23   the privilege by asserting claims the opposing party cannot adequately dispute unless it has access 
24   to the privileged materials.”  Bittaker v. Woodford, 331 F.3d 715, 719 (9th Cir. 2003); see also 
25   Chevron Corp. v. Pennzoil Co., 974 F.2d 1156, 1162 (9th Cir. 1992) (“Where a party raises a 
26   claim which in fairness requires disclosure of the protected communication, the privilege may be 
27   implicitly waived.”).  By contrast, “[a]n express waiver occurs when a party discloses privileged 
1   the privilege by making the information public.”  Bittaker, 331 F.3d at 719.  “A party need not 
2   have intended to waive privilege when it made the disclosure,” Dukes, 2013 WL 1282892 at *7 
3   (citing Weil, 647 F.2d at 24), and “an express waiver need not be effectuated by words or 
4   accompanied by the litigant's subjective intent,” Bittaker, 331 F.3d at 719 n.4. 
5        Similarly, work product protection also may be waived.  Nobles, 422 U.S. at 239.  An 
6   express or voluntary disclosure of work product waives the protection where such disclosure is 
7   made to an adversary in litigation or where the disclosure is made in a manner that substantially 
8   increases the opportunities for potential adversaries to obtain the work product.  Sanmina, 968 
9   F.3d at 1121 (citing 8 Charles Alan Wright & Arthur R. Miller, Federal Practice & Procedure 
10   § 2024 (3d ed. 2020)); see also Nidec Corp. v. Victor Co. of Japan, 249 F.R.D. 575, 578 (N.D. 
11   Cal. 2007) (“[T]he work-product privilege may be waived by disclosure to third parties which 
12   results in disclosure to an adversary party.”).  Work product protection may also be waived 
13   implicitly by putting the protected work product at issue, such as by asserting claims that the 
14   opposing party cannot adequately dispute unless it has access to that protected work product.  See 
15   Bittaker, 331 F.3d at 719; Chevron, 974 F.2d at 1162-63; Sanmina Corp., 968 F.3d at 1124 
16   (“While we are generally guided by the same fairness principle underlying waivers by implication 
17   in the attorney-client privilege context, the overriding concern in the work-product context is not 
18   the confidentiality of a communication, but the protection of the adversary process.”).  Moreover, 
19   even if the protection is not waived, work product may be discoverable if the materials meet the 
20   requirements of Rule 26(b)(1) and if the party seeking production shows a “substantial need for 
21   the materials to prepare its case and cannot, without undue hardship, obtain their substantial 
22   equivalent by other means.”  Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(3)(A).  Upon such a showing, a court must 
23   nevertheless “protect against disclosure of the mental impressions, conclusions, opinions, or legal 
24   theories of a party’s attorney or other representative concerning the litigation,” Fed. R. Civ. P. 
25   26(b)(3)(B).

14        Plaintiff Valeo Schalter und Sensoren GmbH (“Valeo”) and defendant NVIDIA 
15   Corporation (“NVIDIA”) ask the Court to resolve their dispute regarding whether NVIDIA should 
16   be required to periodically update its source code production to account for code developed after 
17   the close of fact discovery.  Dkt. No. 66.  The Court held a hearing on this dispute on August 20, 
18   2024.  Dkt. No. 81.  Upon consideration of the parties’ submission and the arguments presented at 
19   the hearing, the Court denies Valeo’s request for an order requiring NVIDIA to update its source 
20   code production on a monthly basis after the close of fact discovery.  However, as explained 
21   below, NVIDIA is not correct that it has no obligation under Rule 26(e) to supplement its source 
22   code production after the close of fact discovery.                    
23        In this action, Valeo alleges that NVIDIA misappropriated Valeo’s trade secrets relating to 
24   parking and driving assistance technology, in violation of the federal Defend Trade Secrets Act, 18 
25   U.S.C. §§ 1836, 1837, and the California Uniform Trade Secrets Act, Cal. Civ. Code §§ 3426 et 
26   seq.  Dkt. No. 1.  In response to Valeo’s Request for Production (“RFP”) No. 2, NVIDIA has 
27   made source code for an OEM software development project available for inspection, reflecting 
1   OEM project for which NVIDIA is developing software is not yet complete, and NVIDIA 
2   continues to write code.  Id.  Fact discovery closes on October 24, 2024.  Id. at 7. 
3        Valeo argues that because NVIDIA will continue to write code for the OEM project after 
4   fact discovery closes, it should be required to update its source code production after that date by 
5   providing, for example, “monthly updates until the start of production of the [OEM] project.”  Id. 
6   at 2-3 & n.1.  NVIDIA responds that it will continue producing code through the close of fact 
7   discovery, but that it has no obligation to produce code developed after that date because its prior 
8   productions could not be considered incomplete as of the close of fact discovery.  Id. at 6.  
9   NVIDIA also argues that Valeo has no non-speculative basis for suggesting that NVIDIA may 
10   “delay the creation of code incorporating Valeo’s trade secrets until after” the close of fact 
11   discovery.  See id. at 3, 5.                                          
12        Rule 26(e) provides, in relevant part, that a party who has responded to a request for 
13   production must timely supplement or correct its response “if the party learns that in some 
14   material respect the . . . response is incomplete or incorrect, and if the additional or corrective 
15   information has not otherwise been made known to the other parties during the discovery process 
16   or in writing,” or “as ordered by the court.”  Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(e)(1).  The Court agrees with Valeo 
17   that NVIDIA has an affirmative duty to supplement its discovery responses, including its 
18   document production, under Rule 26(e), and that this duty extends past the close of discovery.  See 
19   In re Google RTB Consumer Priv. Litig., No. 21-cv-02155-YGR (VKD), 2023 WL 3046793, at *2 
20   (N.D. Cal. Apr. 21, 2023).  However, NVIDIA’s duty is triggered only if it learns that its prior 
21   production is materially incomplete or incorrect.  Id.                
22        This dispute is unusual in that the discovery material in question—i.e. production of 
23   NVIDIA’s source code responsive to Valeo’s document requests—is not limited to events that 
24   occurred in the past, but encompasses NVIDIA’s alleged ongoing use of Valeo’s trade secrets in 
25   connection with NVIDIA’s work on the OEM project.  These circumstances distinguish this 
26   dispute from cases like Dong Ah Tire & Rubber Co., in which the relevant discovery concerned 
27   events that occurred well before the discovery cutoff date.  See Dong Ah Tire & Rubber Co. v. 
1   (rejecting the contention that relevance alone triggers the duty to supplement); see also id. at *2 
2   (“The duty to supplement under Rule 26(e)(1) is directed to documents generated during the 
3   relevant time frame previously not produced but subsequently discovered.”).  Here, NVIDIA’s 
4   work on the OEM project is expected to continue into 2025, and thus the “relevant time frame” for 
5   this action may extend beyond the current fact discovery deadline.  Dkt. No. 81.  However, as 
6   another judge in this district has observed, “the duty to supplement under Rule 26(e) does not 
7   automatically supersede the fact discovery cutoff as to developments thereafter that relate to prior 
8   requests for discovery made before the cutoff.”  Our Children's Earth v. Leland Stanford Junior 
9   Univ., No. 13-cv-00402-EDL, 2015 WL 12964638, at *3 (N.D. Cal. Oct. 29, 2015); see also In re 
10   Google RTB Consumer Priv. Litig., 2023 WL 3046793, at *2 (“The fact that responsive 
11   documents similar to those previously produced by a custodian have continued to accumulate in 
12   that custodian’s files during the course of litigation does not automatically render the prior 
13   production materially incomplete or incorrect.”).                     
14        The plain language of Rule 26(e)(1) makes clear that the trigger for supplementation is 
15   when a party learns that its prior production is “incomplete” or “inaccurate” “in some material 
16   respect.”  The Court disagrees with NVIDIA that so long as its source production is up-to-date as 
17   of the close of fact discovery, it need not consider whether subsequent changes to the source code 
18   render that prior production an “incomplete” or “inaccurate” representation of the code.  If 
19   NVIDIA makes “material” changes to the responsive portions of the OEM project source code1 
20   after the close of fact discovery, then it will have a duty to supplement its production unless 
21   “additional or corrective information” regarding such material changes has otherwise been made 
22   known to Valeo.  See Switch Communications Group v. Ballard, No. 2:11-cv-00285-KJD, 2012 
23   WL 2342929, at *7 (D. Nev. June 19, 2012) (concluding that Rule 26(e) required defendant to 
24   produce documents generated after its earlier discovery responses “to the extent they materially 
25   affect the completeness or correctness of the previous responses,” such as “documents relating to 
26                                                                         

27                                                                         
    1 The parties’ joint discovery dispute letter alludes to, but does not address, a possible dispute 
    1    continuing efforts to design or build a data center facility that allegedly incorporates [plaintiffs] 
    2  ||  trade secrets”).  If NVIDIA does not make material changes to the responsive portions of the 
    3    source code after the close of fact discovery, then it will have no duty to supplement its 
    4  || production.  Thus, the Court rejects Valeo’s argument that NVIDIA should be required to make 
    5    monthly source code productions after the close of fact discovery, merely because NVIDIA 
    6  || continues to work on that code. 
    7          As discussed at the hearing, the Court encourages the parties to consider and agree upon a 
    8  ||  date after the close of fact discovery on which NVIDIA will make a supplemental production of 
    9    responsive portions of its source code, if warranted under Rule 26(e), with a view toward avoiding 
   10  ||  disruption of other pretrial deadlines (e.g. expert disclosures) set by the presiding judge.

21   I.   BACKGROUND                                                       
22        Valeo employed Mr. Mohamed Shawki Elamir as a systems engineer in Germany for

11   II.  LEGAL STANDARD                                                   
12        The Hague Convention on the Taking of Evidence Abroad in Civil or Commercial Matters, 
13   March 8, 1970, 23 U.S.T. 2555, T.I.A.S. No. 7444 (“Hague Evidence Convention” or 
14   “Convention”), “prescribes certain procedures by which a judicial authority in one contracting 
15   state may request evidence located in another contracting state.”  Societe Nationale Industrielle 
16   Aerospatiale v. U.S. Dist. Ct. for S. Dist. of Iowa, 482 U.S. 522, 524 (1987).  A federal district 
17   court may transmit a “letter of request” for evidence directly to the Central Authority designated 
18   by another party to the Convention for execution.  See Hague Evidence Convention, Art. 2; 28 
19   U.S.C. § 1781(b)(2).  The United States and Germany are both signatories to the Convention.  See 
20   https://www.hcch.net/en/instruments/conventions/status-table/?cid=82.   
21        Where the requirements of the Convention are met, courts in the Ninth Circuit generally 
22   grant motions requesting issuance of a letter of request, unless the opposing party identifies a good 
23   reason to deny the application.  See Successor Agency to Former Emeryville Redevelopment 
24   Agency v. Swagelok Co., No. 17-cv-00308-WHO, 2020 WL 7042860, at *2 (N.D. Cal. Dec. 1, 
25   2020) (citing S.E.C. v. Leslie, 07-cv-03444 JF (PVT), 2009 WL 688836, at *2 (N.D. Cal. Mar. 16, 
26   2009)); see also WebPros Int’l, LLC v. Asli, No. 22-cv-01963-IM, 2024 WL 3064985, at *2 (D. 
27   Or. June 20, 2024) (summarizing cases).  Like all discovery, such motions must comply with the 
1   nonprivileged matter that is relevant to any party’s claim or defense.”  Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b).  
2   Likewise, a motion for issuance of a letter of request is subject to the case management schedule 
3   set by the district court.                                            
4   III.  DISCUSSION                                                      
5        NVIDIA objects to issuance of Valeo’s proposed letter of request on the ground that Valeo 
6   unduly delayed bringing its motion, such that the documents it seeks could not be obtained until 
7   after the close of fact discovery.  In addition, the Court raised sua sponte whether the proposed 
8   letter of request complies with the requirements of the Hague Evidence Convention, in view of 
9   Germany’s declarations.  The Court address both issues.               
10        A.   Whether Valeo’s Motion Is Untimely                          
11        Civil Local Rule 37-3 provides that “[d]iscovery requests that call for responses . . . after 
12   the applicable discovery cut-off are not enforceable, except by order of the Court for good cause 
13   shown.”  Civil L.R. 37-3.  NVIDIA observes that because Valeo did not file its motion until 
14   November 18, 2024, one month before the December 18, 2024 close of fact discovery, the motion 
15   could not be heard, and the letter of request could not issue, until after the fact discovery cut-off.  
16   Dkt. No. 161 at 3-4; see also Civil L.R. 7-2(a) (requiring 35 days’ notice for hearings on motions). 
17        According to NVIDIA, Valeo has known since at least May 30, 2024 that its former 
18   employee, Mr. Elamir, worked on the same functionality that Mr. Moniruzzaman had previously 
19   worked on, see Dkt. No. 161 at 1; Dkt. No. 162-2 (amended response to Interrogatory No. 2), and 
20   Valeo has known “for years” that after Mr. Elamir left Valeo’s employ, he worked for Mercedes, 
21   see Dkt. No. 161 at 2; Dkt. No. 161-3.                                
22        Valeo does not dispute that since at least July 2024 it had knowledge of Mr. Elamir’s 
23   employment at Mercedes and his subsequent role at NVIDIA, including the specific work Mr. 
24   Elamir performed on NVIDIA’s source code.  See Dkt. No. 164 at 2.  Valeo’s arguments that it 
25   required more information regarding Mr. Elamir’s “recruitment and hiring” by NVIDIA before it 
26   could reasonably seek documents from Mercedes, see id. at 2, 4, are not persuasive for at least two 
27   reasons.  First, several of the document requests in Valeo’s proposed letter of request have nothing 
1   trade secrets in aid of NVIDIA’s performance of its contract with Mercedes.  See Dkt. No. 152 at 
2   3-5.  Yet, Valeo has known since early 2021 of NVIDIA’s contract to supply advanced parking 
3   and driving assistance software to Mercedes and that Mercedes would have information regarding 
4   NVIDIA’s performance of that contract.  See id. at 2; Dkt. No. 1 ¶¶ 9-10, 50, 53.  Second, to the

9   164 at 2.  In these circumstances, Valeo has not shown good cause for waiting until November 18, 
10   2024 to seek issuance of a letter of request directed to Mercedes, knowing that if the motion was 
11   granted, such letter would not be issued until after the December 18, 2024 close of fact discovery.2

13   request does not seek discovery, but rather impeachment evidence or evidence to refresh

16   any specific evidence in Mercedes’s possession, but instead describes categories of documents that

19   152-1 at 2 (“This Letter of Request is of an urgent nature as the discovery in this matter will close 
20   on December 18th, 2024.”).

22   in Mercedes’s possession was not timely filed, and no good cause excuses Valeo’s delay.

11   II.  LEGAL STANDARD                                                   
12        The Hague Convention on the Taking of Evidence Abroad in Civil or Commercial Matters, 
13   March 8, 1970, 23 U.S.T. 2555, T.I.A.S. No. 7444 (“Hague Evidence Convention” or 
14   “Convention”), “prescribes certain procedures by which a judicial authority in one contracting 
15   state may request evidence located in another contracting state.”  Societe Nationale Industrielle 
16   Aerospatiale v. U.S. Dist. Ct. for S. Dist. of Iowa,
482 U.S. 522
, 524 (1987).  A federal district 
17   court may transmit a “letter of request” for evidence directly to the Central Authority designated 
18   by another party to the Convention for execution.  See Hague Evidence Convention, Art. 2; 28
19 U.S.C. § 1781
(b)(2).  The United States and Germany are both signatories to the Convention.  See 
20   https://www.hcch.net/en/instruments/conventions/status-table/?cid=82.   
21        Where the requirements of the Convention are met, courts in the Ninth Circuit generally 
22   grant motions requesting issuance of a letter of request, unless the opposing party identifies a good 
23   reason to deny the application.  See Successor Agency to Former Emeryville Redevelopment

8   letter of request complies with the requirements of the Hague Evidence Convention, in view of 
9   Germany’s declarations.  The Court address both issues.

11        Civil Local Rule 37-3 provides that “[d]iscovery requests that call for responses . . . after 
12   the applicable discovery cut-off are not enforceable, except by order of the Court for good cause 
13   shown.”  Civil L.R. 37-3.  NVIDIA observes that because Valeo did not file its motion until 
14   November 18, 2024, one month before the December 18, 2024 close of fact discovery, the motion 
15   could not be heard, and the letter of request could not issue, until after the fact discovery cut-off.

21   see Dkt. No. 161 at 2; Dkt. No. 161-3.

23   employment at Mercedes and his subsequent role at NVIDIA, including the specific work Mr. 
24   Elamir performed on NVIDIA’s source code.  See Dkt. No. 164 at 2.  Valeo’s arguments that it 
25   required more information regarding Mr. Elamir’s “recruitment and hiring” by NVIDIA before it 
26   could reasonably seek documents from Mercedes, see

; Dkt. No. 1 ¶¶ 9-10, 50, 53.  Second, to the

8   has known since July 2024 the nature of Mr. Elamir’s subsequent work for NVIDIA.  See Dkt. No. 
9   164 at 2.  In these circumstances, Valeo has not shown good cause for waiting until November 18, 
10   2024 to seek issuance of a letter of request directed to Mercedes, knowing that if the motion was 
11   granted, such letter would not be issued until after the December 18, 2024 close of fact discovery.2 
12        When pressed on the timing of its motion at the hearing, Valeo explained that its letter of 
13   request does not seek discovery, but rather impeachment evidence or evidence to refresh 
14   recollection at trial.  Dkt. No. 180.  However, while Valeo (like all litigants) may expect to use 
15   some of the documents it requests from Mercedes at trial, the letter of request does not identify 
16   any specific evidence in Mercedes’s possession, but instead describes categories of documents that 
17   may exist.  See Dkt. No. 152 at 3-4.  This is classic pretrial discovery.  Moreover, the proposed 
18   letter clearly contemplates obtaining any responsive documents as part of discovery.  See Dkt. No. 
19   152-1 at 2 (“This Letter of Request is of an urgent nature as the discovery in this matter will close 
20   on December 18th, 2024.”).                                            
21        The Court concludes that Valeo’s motion for issuance of a letter of request for documents 
22   in Mercedes’s possession was not timely filed, and no good cause excuses Valeo’s delay.
